record.paper_title: Exploring Progressions: A Collection of Problems
record.original_question: Let α, β, and γ be distinct real numbers that are consecutive terms of a harmonic progression. Prove that α, α − γ, and α − β are also consecutive terms of a harmonic progression.

evidence.quote: If the distinct reals α, β, γ are consecutive terms of a harmonic progression then the same is true for the numbers α, α − γ, α − β.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Three nonzero real numbers x, y, z are said to be consecutive terms of a harmonic progression if their reciprocals 1/x, 1/y, 1/z are consecutive terms of an arithmetic progression, i.e. 2/y = 1/x + 1/z.

Let α, β, γ be three distinct real numbers (all nonzero) that are consecutive terms of a harmonic progression. Prove that the three numbers α, α − γ, α − β are also consecutive terms of a harmonic progression; that is, show that
   2/(α − γ) = 1/α + 1/(α − β).
artifact.status_search_result: This is a classical elementary algebra exercise on harmonic progressions with a short direct proof: from 2/β = 1/α + 1/γ one derives β = 2αγ/(α+γ), and substituting yields 1/α + 1/(α−β) = 2/(α−γ). The result is established by routine computation and is considered solved.

status_evidence.title: Direct verification
status_evidence.snippet: From 2/β = 1/α + 1/γ one obtains β = 2αγ/(α+γ); then α−β = α(α−γ)/(α+γ) and 2α−β = 2α²/(α+γ), giving 1/α + 1/(α−β) = (2α−β)/(α(α−β)) = 2/(α−γ).
status_evidence.claim: The identity follows from elementary algebraic manipulation, so the problem is a solved exercise.
